resources.string: See which agents need you, read their work and reply on your own machines.
Linux or WSL running herdr-core and OpenSSH, on the same Wi-Fi or VPN as your phone.
kudde uses your password once, or you run one command yourself.
kudde checks the machine and shows how many agents run there.
Hear when an agent needs you, also with kudde closed.
Add a machine that runs herdr-core to see its agents here.
The machine\'s name on your network or VPN, or its IP address.
How kudde lists this machine. Leave it empty to use the address.
Tailscale SSH does not work with the phone key: use an address and port where OpenSSH answers.
Still no answer. This can take 20 seconds.
On %1$s, signed in as %2$s, paste this into a terminal and press Enter:
Sending it to yourself in a note or a message is fine: nothing in it is secret.

It adds this phone\'s key, then prints the machine\'s host key. With this key, SSH runs only herdr-core: no terminal session, no forwarding. herdr-core can still run commands as that user, so treat the key like a shell login.
First connection to %1$s. The command you ran there printed its host key. Trust it only if the fingerprint is the same:
Not the same? Do not trust it. Something else answered at that address: Tailscale SSH, or another SSH server on that port.
Choose how to add it, signed in as %1$s.
%1$s did not accept the phone key.
Choose how to add it, signed in as %2$s. If you already ran the command, check that its quotes arrived unchanged, then try again.
Install it there as %2$s, then try again. The setup guide has the command.
kudde signs in once as %1$s with that account\'s password, adds the same key and signs out. The password is not stored.
Run one command at the machine. kudde never sees a password.
Both ways add only this phone\'s public key, limited to herdr-core. Existing keys stay in place.
No agents are running there yet. One you start at your desk in herdr shows up here by itself.
kudde can tell you when an agent needs you or has finished, also while the app is closed.
It needs two things: a UnifiedPush app such as ntfy on this phone, and kudde-push running on %1$s. The setup guide shows how to install kudde-push.
No test alert from %1$s within 30 seconds.
Check that kudde-push runs there; the setup guide shows how.
Alerts need a UnifiedPush app, such as ntfy. Install one, then try again.
Notifications are not allowed for kudde.
Alerts are already on for this phone.
To let this phone into a machine, run this there, signed in as the user your agents run under:
Opens the step this machine is at
Swipe sideways for other panes in this tab. At either end it bounces; with one pane it only bounces.
Swipe up: the next agent that needs you. Down: back.
Tap the map: every pane of the tab.
With TalkBack, the title bar\'s actions move around: Next terminal, Previous terminal, Next agent that needs you, Previous agent that needs you. Double tap the map for every pane of the tab.
First connection to %1$s. If this key is not your machine\'s, whoever answered gets the password, and setup can still look as if it worked. Trust it only if you are sure.
Your first machine is set up.
%1$s did not accept the password for %2$s.
Check it and try again. Nothing was changed there.
Some machines lock an account after a few wrong tries. To be safe, choose "Add it yourself" to run the command at the machine.
%1$s does not take a password over SSH.
Choose "Add it yourself" to run the command at the machine: it needs none.
%1$s asks for more than a password, such as a code.
Choose "Add it yourself" to run the command at the machine.
The connection to %1$s dropped while the key was being added.
kudde cannot tell whether it went in. Try again: adding it twice does no harm.
The setup on %1$s ended with code %2$d.
Choose "Add it yourself" to run the command at the machine to see why.
Stopped before the key was added.
kudde had signed in to %1$s and signed out again. Nothing was changed there.
The key was added before it stopped.
kudde is connecting to %1$s with it.
kudde added the key, but %1$s still refuses it.
The SSH server may read keys from another file, or refuse the home directory\'s permissions (StrictModes). The setup guide\'s check script finds out which.
